title: IB Social and Cultural Anthropology Revision Plan:…
summary: IB Social and Cultural Anthropology revision plan for November: three flexible weeks of topic triage, ethnography, timed practice and rest across subjects.
body_markdown:
Three weeks before an exam, a folder full of notes can feel reassuring until you try to write an answer without it. This **IB Social and Cultural Anthropology revision plan** turns those notes into usable arguments: spend the first week finding gaps, the second applying ethnography to questions, and the third rehearsing timed responses while protecting rest.


For November candidates balancing several subjects, flexibility matters. Count backwards from your first anthropology examination, using your school’s confirmed timetable. Treat the sessions below as movable blocks. A demanding day in another subject might leave room for only fifteen minutes of anthropology retrieval.


**Your starting checklist**


Before beginning, gather:


- Your SL or HL assessment guidance and confirmed examination dates.
- Your studied ethnographies, class notes and teacher feedback.
- Official examination questions and their accompanying markschemes, obtained through your school or authorised access.
- A single page for recording errors and the next action each requires.


As a starting allocation, aim for four focused anthropology sessions each week, plus brief retrieval on selected days. Adjust this around your other subjects and current weaknesses. A useful session produces something you can assess: an essay plan, a comparison or a response to an unfamiliar extract.


**Week one: identify what you can actually use**


Start by checking the assessment demands. Under the[IB’s current anthropology assessment guidance](https://ibpublishing.ibo.org/exinst/apps/exinst/pdf.html?doc=EX_instructions_2026_e&part=10&chapter=10) , Paper 1 lasts 90 minutes at SL and two hours at HL. Paper 2 lasts 90 minutes at SL and two and a half hours at HL. Confirm that this guidance applies to your examination session with your teacher.


Paper 2 includes a compulsory Section A response connecting a specified key concept, a real-world issue and ethnographic material. Section B requires one essay at SL and two essays from different areas of inquiry at HL. HL students also need dedicated Paper 1 preparation for anthropological ethics.


This makes topic triage more precise than simply choosing your favourite ethnography. Use the[overview of anthropology topics and areas of inquiry](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-social-cultural-anthropology-topics-full-list) alongside your course materials to map your coverage.


For each studied area, ask yourself:


- Can I explain its central debates without looking?
- Can I recall specific ethnographic evidence and its context?
- Can I connect that evidence to a concept and construct an argument?


Mark each area green, amber or red. Prioritise amber areas where focused work can make your evidence usable, while repairing red gaps that threaten required coverage. Keep all nine key concepts in rotation. The IB guidance expects preparation across three areas of inquiry at SL and four at HL, so maintain breadth while deepening your strongest material.


Build a compact evidence sheet for each ethnography: anthropologist, location, research context, methods, two or three precise examples, relevant concepts and limitations. Include how the researcher’s position may have shaped the account. Avoid turning this into another transcription exercise.


Finish the week with a short diagnostic response. If unfamiliar terminology keeps interrupting your writing, the[guide to common anthropology learning difficulties](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-social-cultural-anthropology-first-term-struggles) can help you identify what needs rebuilding. Use Study Notes to clarify a gap, then Flashcards to test whether you can retrieve the explanation later.


An observer studies a student drinking tea at a desk covered with books.


**Week two: turn knowledge into answers**


The second week should expose the distance between recognising an idea and explaining it under pressure.


Alternate Paper 1 and Paper 2 practice. For Paper 1, work with unfamiliar extracts and practise identifying what the text supports. Separate the author’s evidence from your interpretation. HL students should also rehearse ethical analysis: identify who could be affected, explain competing responsibilities and consider the consequences of research decisions.


For Paper 2, select an official examination question and spend ten minutes planning before writing. Establish your argument, choose the evidence that advances it and explain the connection. An ethnographic example earns its place through the analytical work it does.


Practise the compulsory Section A task explicitly. Choose from the concepts and issues offered in the question, ground the issue in a specific contemporary example, and connect it to your studied material. Check that your response develops those relationships rather than presenting three separate descriptions.


Use examination materials in three ways across the week: one question for diagnosis, another for a timed response, and a third for planning only. This preserves practice time for feedback and repair. Match materials to your syllabus and level; older formats may require your teacher’s guidance.


After each written response, record the most consequential weakness. “Need more detail” is difficult to act on. “Add a specific observation and explain how it supports the claim about power” gives your next session a purpose.


RevisionDojo’s AI Chat and Grading tools can support explanation and feedback, but compare suggestions with your teacher’s guidance and official criteria. If research methods remain unclear, selected[SL anthropology coursework examples](https://www.revisiondojo.com/coursework-exemplars/social-and-cultural-anthropology-ia-sl/grade-6) in the Coursework Library can provide material for discussing research choices. Coursework criteria differ from examination criteria, so keep that distinction clear.


**Week three: rehearse, repair and recover**


Early in the final week, complete a timed paper in your level’s full duration. Schedule another paper on a separate day if your wider timetable allows. Preserve time to review both; an unchecked script leaves its most useful information unread.


Practise selecting questions, allocating time and finishing responses. HL students should check that their two Section B choices come from different areas of inquiry. Use the markscheme and criteria to distinguish missing knowledge from weak application or incomplete reasoning.


Repair recurring problems with short tasks. Rewrite one analytical paragraph. Retrieve an ethnography’s context without notes. Plan a comparison using a different concept. The[anthropology revision resource collection](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/tag/ib-social-and-cultural-anthropology) can help you locate targeted explanations without restarting the whole course.


Protect an evening away from anthropology and keep your usual sleep routine. On a day dominated by another subject’s exam, move the longer session or replace it with brief retrieval. Avoid creating a backlog that forces several full papers into the final days.


In the last 24 hours, review your evidence sheets, recurring errors and examination logistics. Leave unfamiliar material for another time unless it closes an essential gap.


**Make the next session concrete**


Three weeks become manageable when each session has a clear output. RevisionDojo brings revision resources together so you can move from clarification to practice without repeatedly rebuilding your plan. Use Tutors for a persistent conceptual difficulty, and treat Predicted Papers and Mock Exams as additional rehearsal rather than forecasts of November questions.


Start with the weakness your diagnostic exposed: **practise in the Questionbank, then sit timed papers in Exam mode** . Review the result, choose one repair and give yourself enough rest to return ready to use it.
